title: Russia launches mass production of electronic warfare systems to counter Starlink, but analysts say its capabilities are overstated
gist: Russia's newly mass-produced Volna Kupol Garant jammer, marketed as a 'Starlink killer,' actually covers only about 20 square kilometers at roughly $1.5 million per unit and cannot plausibly disrupt satellites in orbit per multiple independent analysts, while its own active jamming signal makes it a detectable, targetable beacon - and Russia is signaling plans to export the technology, including to partners already tied to Iranian missile and drone programs.

insights.claim: Russia's Volna Kupol Garant electronic-warfare system, aimed at jamming Starlink, is not mobile, costs about $1.5 million per unit, and covers only about 20 square kilometers (roughly a 2.5km radius) - a cost/coverage ratio RUSI's Dr. Thomas Withington calls financially unsustainable for scaling across occupied Ukrainian territory.
insights.speaker: Thomas Withington
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete cost-per-coverage-area benchmark showing the system cannot achieve wide-area denial economically, useful for assessing the credibility of Russian EW mass-production claims.
insights.quote: Twenty square kilometers isn't that much. It's a range of 2.5 kilometers, which is nothing. And $1.5 million dollars to jam 20 square kilometers — that's very expensive.

insights.claim: Ukrainian EW specialist Serhii 'Flash' Beskrestnov reported that eight of the system's antenna dishes were enough to 'deafen' a passing Starlink satellite and destabilize terminal operation across roughly 20 square kilometers, by directing interference at the satellite so it cannot receive signals from ordinary ground terminals.
insights.speaker: Serhii Beskrestnov
insights.so_what: Describes the specific technical mechanism (terminal-to-satellite uplink jamming, not satellite destruction) by which the system actually degrades Starlink service.
insights.locator: What do we know about Volna Kupol Garant?

themes.theme: Expert skepticism on the 'Starlink killer' claim

insights.claim: Thomas Withington is skeptical of Russia's claim that the system can directly disrupt Starlink satellites in orbit, arguing it would require an enormous, hard-to-generate ground signal power to reach and damage a satellite roughly 1,000 kilometers up, and that generating such power would both overload the system's electrical infrastructure and reveal its location.
insights.speaker: Thomas Withington
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts Kremlin media's 'Starlink killer' framing with a physics-based argument, useful for discounting exaggerated Russian EW capability claims in future reporting.
insights.quote: For the signal to be powerful enough to jam a signal in space, you need a huge amount of power on the ground.

insights.claim: Anton Zemlianyi of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center argues there is no solid basis to claim Volna Kupol Garant can directly affect satellites in orbit - such systems create ground-level interference ('white noise') that disrupts terminal-to-satellite communication, comparable to a conventional electronic-warfare system disrupting a drone's control-channel link to its operator, without touching the satellite itself.
insights.speaker: Anton Zemlianyi
insights.so_what: Clarifies the actual operating mechanism (link disruption, not satellite damage) which investors and analysts should use to correctly assess EW system capability claims in general.
insights.quote: The main task of such a system is to create interference and overload the necessary frequency range.

insights.claim: Zemlianyi argues the claimed coverage of Volna Kupol Garant is in line with existing Russian tactical electronic-warfare systems and is not a fundamentally new threat, and that mass production alone will not shift the front-line balance - what matters is how quickly Russia integrates the systems and how quickly Ukraine adapts.
insights.speaker: Anton Zemlianyi
insights.so_what: Suggests scaling production of an already-known capability class is a lower-signal event than headlines suggest; the decisive variable is integration speed and counter-adaptation, not unit count.

themes.theme: Real but limited battlefield effect, and self-exposure risk

insights.claim: Ukrainian soldiers, per Spain's El Mundo, acknowledge that Russian electronic-warfare systems of this type do measurably reduce Starlink's effectiveness on parts of the front, prompting Ukraine to prioritize development of its own independent satellite communications system as the more reliable long-term fix.
insights.speaker: The Insider
insights.so_what: Confirms the jammer has real, if partial, tactical effect - Ukraine is treating satellite-communications diversification (not just counter-jamming) as the durable solution.
insights.locator: In an interview with Spain's El Mundo

insights.claim: Samuel Bendett (CNA) notes that by emitting a powerful jamming signal, Volna Kupol Garant itself becomes a detectable 'beacon,' making it trackable and ultimately a target for enemy strikes - a vulnerability shared with radar and other signal-emitting combat systems.
insights.speaker: Samuel Bendett
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural counter-battery vulnerability inherent to active jammers, consistent with reported Ukrainian strikes already destroying deployed units.
insights.locator: Bendett also noted another important nuance

insights.claim: Multiple Volna Kupol Garant units have already been destroyed by Ukrainian strikes, based on OSINT imagery cited in the report, including a unit deployed near Gelendzhik - consistent with the system's fixed, non-mobile, signal-emitting design making it locatable and vulnerable once operational.
insights.speaker: The Insider
insights.so_what: Provides concrete evidence the system's operational vulnerability is not theoretical - it is already being neutralized in the field.
insights.locator: The Volna Kupol Garant system deployed near Gelendzhik

insights.claim: Zemlianyi expects such systems to be deployed mainly near critical sites in occupied territory and border areas rather than as continuous front-wide coverage, since blanket saturation of the front and rear would require prohibitively large resources.
insights.speaker: Anton Zemlianyi
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for where these systems will actually be concentrated (critical infrastructure/border zones) rather than uniformly across the front.
insights.quote: That will probably become the main task, since Russia will not be able to create continuous electronic warfare coverage over large areas.

insights.claim: A TASS source in Russia's defense industry signaled Moscow may export Volna Kupol Garant-type technology to 'all interested countries,' noting similar tools have already appeared in China - a statement CNA's Samuel Bendett called 'concerning' given reported Russian assistance to Iran on supersonic cruise missile development and drone strikes on CIA facilities in the Persian Gulf region.
insights.speaker: Samuel Bendett
insights.so_what: Flags a proliferation pathway for Russian EW/anti-satellite jamming technology to China and Iran, relevant to broader assessments of adversary counter-space and counter-Starlink capability spread.
insights.quote: The most interesting thing is that Russia reserves the right to spread this technology among all interested countries around the world.
